title: Chapter 167: Dresser
html:
The nurse will return after dispensing the medicine. Once she discovers the notebook missing, she’ll search for it. But she seems only slightly stronger than Xiaoxiao or the Pen Spirit. In a direct fight, I might win.

Hammer ready, Chen Ge advanced. Most people would have been paralyzed by shock long ago, unable to reason or plan. He continued opening rooms one by one but found nothing until he reached the third-floor bathroom.

The door opened somewhere downstairs, so this bathroom shouldn’t contain the “door.”

The white cat’s anxiety pressed against his shoulder. When Chen Ge pushed inside, absolute darkness swallowed the beam of his flashlight.

A row of squat toilets looked sinister in the gloom. Unlike the school cubicles, these had no locks, probably so staff could intervene during emergencies. He searched each one but found nothing unusual, then stopped at the sinks and noticed the mirror’s peculiar design.

A curtain hung above the glass, positioned to cover it with a single pull. The detail reminded him of his Haunted House. The mirrors here must have caused problems too.

He drew up the curtain. Handprints and greasy smears covered the mirror so densely that his reflection barely showed.

The door isn’t here.After confirming the bathroom’s layout, he returned to the corridor and descended the nearby stairs.

The lower he went, the stronger the stench became. On the second floor, strange changes had appeared across the walls and corridor.

Whether from age or something less natural, sections of wall bulged outward with a reddish tint, like bruised flesh. Dark residue clung to cracks in the floor, as though blood had seeped up and dried there.

The second floor felt entirely different. If the third had been eerie, this level was openly dangerous, its threat almost doubled. Every instinct urged him to turn and run.

Could that truly be blood?He lifted a piece of the dark residue and crushed it between his fingers. No metallic smell. Probably ordinary red clay.

Mattresses obstructed the corridor, and he ripped several open as he passed. The closer he descended toward the first floor, the more lifelike their dolls felt—not in appearance, but in the presence they radiated.

By the first floor, will the dolls crawl out by themselves?

He considered the possibility seriously. Near the corridor’s corner, several unusual rooms caught his attention. Every patient-room door had a viewing window for staff, but these did not.

The director’s office?He had explored nearly the entire hospital without seeing another labeled door. Inside was an enormous office created by demolishing the walls between three ordinary rooms.

Pots of dead plants lined one wall beside empty bookcases and a desk. A rest area occupied half as much space as the office itself, containing a single bed and an absurdly large wardrobe.

After closing the door, Chen Ge stepped among patient files scattered across the floor. Unlike the records in the nurse’s notebook, these remained unaltered, suggesting their subjects were still alive.

The hospital had operated for at least a decade and treated far more patients than Chen Ge expected. Though psychiatric patients formed only a fraction of Jiujiang’s millions, the city had just two licensed public hospitals, with a combined capacity of roughly a thousand. Many conditions also required repeated treatment. Demand therefore exceeded capacity, creating a market for private institutions such as the Jiujiang Third Psychological Convalescence Centre.

It possessed the required licenses but remained a private business driven by profit and plagued by poor management. Because psychiatric patients could struggle to report mistreatment, serious abuses were easily ignored. Admitting the mentally healthy Wang Haiming was one example.

After skimming several files, Chen Ge lost interest. The diagnoses were nearly identical, as were the prescribed treatments.

“Doctor Gao is a real physician. These people merely crushed their patients’ wills and reduced them to empty puppets.”

He searched the empty bookshelves and desk drawers, then overturned the bed in the rest area. Nothing. Only the suspiciously large wardrobe remained.

“Two adults could fit inside. Did someone hide the missing director here?”

Hammer raised, he inspected it. Police tape sealed the doors, its undisturbed edges showing that no one had opened it since.

“Why would the police seal a wardrobe? Was there a body inside?”

More peculiar details emerged. Duct tape covered every seam, strange incantations marked the corners, and red nails half a palm long protruded from the wood.

“Whatever is inside must be important.” Chen Ge lowered the white cat beside the entrance, tore away the police tape, and pried open the door with his mallet.

No corpse or bizarre collection waited inside—only several pages covered in writing and a stack of unsent letters. The first line on the top sheet made his heart jump.

“The kid inside Room 3 is acting up again. He is the first person to have seen the ‘door’, so I suspect the appearance of the ‘door’ is related to him.”

Wasn’t Room 3 supposed to be empty? Where did this child come from?

As he read on, the letters revealed how a single “door” had brought the entire hospital to ruin.
